note: Landing / impact coordinates: Moon in selenographic degrees (east positive), Mars in planetocentric degrees (east positive). 'approx' = location only known roughly. Compiled for Ember Atlas Labs, Team Ainexa, Nov 2026.

items.name: Ranger 7
items.kid: Ranger 7 flew straight at the Moon on purpose. In its last 17 minutes it sent back more than 4,000 photos, each one closer than the last, until it hit the ground.
items.science: The first close-up pictures of the Moon showed craters as small as a metre, so engineers knew what landers would face.
items.fact: The area where it hit was later named Mare Cognitum: 'the Sea that has become known'.

items.name: Ranger 8
items.kid: Ranger 8 took 7,000 pictures of the Sea of Tranquility as it dived toward it, then crashed.
items.science: Its photos helped choose the flat plain where Apollo 11 would land four years later.
items.fact: It hit only about 70 km from where Neil Armstrong would later step out.

items.name: Ranger 9
items.kid: Ranger 9 crashed inside a big crater called Alphonsus. TV stations showed its pictures live, so people at home watched the Moon get closer and closer.
items.science: Its sharp images of a crater floor helped scientists study how the Moon's surface formed.
items.fact: It was the first live TV broadcast from a spacecraft approaching another world.

items.name: Surveyor 1
items.kid: Surveyor 1 was America's first soft landing on the Moon. It touched down gently on three legs and sent home over 11,000 pictures.
items.science: It proved the Moon's ground was firm enough to hold a spacecraft, not deep soft dust.
items.fact: It landed on its very first try, in 1966, three years before Apollo 11.

items.name: Surveyor 3
items.kid: Surveyor 3 bounced twice when it landed and then dug little trenches with a scoop. Two years later, Apollo 12 astronauts walked over and cut parts off it to bring home!
items.science: Parts brought back by Apollo 12 showed how metal, glass and paint change after years on the Moon.
items.fact: It is the only robot on the Moon that astronauts have ever visited.

items.name: Surveyor 5
items.kid: Surveyor 5 landed on a slope in the Sea of Tranquility and tested what the soil was made of.
items.science: It found the Moon's dark 'seas' are made of basalt, the same volcanic rock as Hawaii.
items.fact: Engineers fixed a fuel leak during the trip by inventing a new landing plan in a few days.

items.name: Surveyor 6
items.kid: Surveyor 6 did something amazing: it fired its engines and hopped about 2.5 metres to a new spot.
items.science: The hop was the first lift-off from the Moon, showing that rockets could take off again from its surface.
items.fact: That little hop, in 1967, was the first time anything launched from another world.

items.name: Surveyor 7
items.kid: Surveyor 7 landed in the rocky highlands near the bright crater Tycho, far from the flat seas.
items.science: It showed the highlands are made of lighter, different rock than the dark seas.
items.fact: It spotted laser beams fired at it from telescopes on Earth.

items.name: Apollo 11 · Tranquility Base
items.kid: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed here and became the first people to walk on the Moon. They left the bottom half of their lander, a flag, footprints and a mirror box.
items.science: The mirror box (a laser retroreflector) still bounces lasers back to Earth, measuring the Moon's distance to a few millimetres.
items.fact: The Moon is moving away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year: we know because of these mirrors.

items.name: Apollo 12 · Ocean of Storms
items.kid: Pete Conrad and Alan Bean made a pinpoint landing just 180 metres from Surveyor 3. They set up science instruments that radioed data home for years.
items.science: Its seismometer felt 'moonquakes' and showed the Moon rings like a bell when something hits it.
items.fact: Conrad, the shortest astronaut, joked as he stepped down: 'that may have been a small one for Neil, but that's a long one for me'.

items.name: Apollo 14 · Fra Mauro
items.kid: Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell explored hilly ground and pulled a little cart of tools. Shepard even hit two golf balls!
items.science: It left a second laser mirror and brought back rocks from deep inside the Moon thrown out by a giant impact.
items.fact: One golf ball has been found in modern photos, about 40 metres from where it was hit.

items.name: Apollo 15 · Hadley-Apennine
items.kid: Dave Scott and Jim Irwin landed between tall mountains and a long winding canyon called Hadley Rille. They were the first to drive a car on the Moon.
items.science: They found the 'Genesis Rock', a piece of the Moon's very first crust, about 4 billion years old.
items.fact: Scott dropped a hammer and a feather together: with no air, they hit the ground at the same time, just as Galileo predicted.

items.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle 1 (Apollo 15)
items.kid: The first Moon buggy! It folded up like a beach chair inside the lander and drove 28 km with two astronauts on board.
items.science: Driving let astronauts reach rocks kilometres away, so they collected far more varied samples.
items.fact: It is still parked there, with its TV camera pointed at the lander so mission control could watch the lift-off.

items.name: Apollo 16 · Descartes Highlands
items.kid: John Young and Charlie Duke explored the bright highlands. Duke left a photo of his family on the ground with a note on the back.
items.science: Scientists expected volcanoes here but found smashed-up impact rock, which changed ideas about how the highlands formed.
items.fact: They set a Moon speed record of about 18 km/h in their rover.

items.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle 2 (Apollo 16)
items.kid: The second Moon buggy carried Young and Duke 27 km across hills and craters.
items.science: It carried tools, cameras and samples, turning each moonwalk into a long field trip.
items.fact: Its wheels were made of woven piano wire instead of rubber tyres.

items.name: Apollo 17 · Taurus-Littrow
items.kid: Gene Cernan and geologist Harrison Schmitt spent three days in a deep valley. Cernan was the last person to walk on the Moon, so far.
items.science: Schmitt found orange soil made of tiny glass beads from ancient fire-fountain volcanoes.
items.fact: They fixed a broken rover fender with maps and duct tape.

items.name: Lunar Roving Vehicle 3 (Apollo 17)
items.kid: The last Moon buggy drove the longest: about 36 km across the valley of Taurus-Littrow.
items.science: It reached the valley's mountains, where the crew picked up rocks from a huge ancient landslide.
items.fact: Its camera filmed the lander blasting off the Moon, the last view of the Apollo era.

items.name: LCROSS impact
items.kid: NASA smashed an empty rocket stage into a dark crater near the Moon's south pole, and a small spacecraft flew through the dust cloud to sniff it.
items.science: It found water ice in the crater, which could one day give astronauts water, air and rocket fuel.
items.fact: The crater, Cabeus, is so deep in shadow that sunlight has not touched its floor for billions of years.

items.name: GRAIL Ebb & Flow
items.kid: Two twin spacecraft, Ebb and Flow, chased each other around the Moon to map its gravity. At the end they were steered into a mountain on purpose.
items.science: They made the best gravity map of any world, revealing cracks and buried structures under the surface.
items.fact: The crash site is named after Sally Ride, the first American woman in space.

items.name: LADEE
items.kid: LADEE was about the size of a small car. It flew very low to study the Moon's super-thin air and floating dust, then crashed on the far side.
items.science: It measured the Moon's thin atmosphere of helium, argon and neon, and how meteor showers kick up dust.
items.fact: It also tested laser messages from Earth to the Moon, much faster than radio.

items.name: IM-1 Odysseus (NASA CLPS)
items.kid: Odysseus, built by the company Intuitive Machines, carried NASA instruments to near the Moon's south pole. It tipped onto its side when it landed but still sent data!
items.science: It tested new landing sensors and studied the south pole region where future astronauts may live.
items.fact: It was the first US Moon landing since Apollo 17, 51 years earlier.

items.name: Blue Ghost Mission 1 (NASA CLPS)
items.kid: Blue Ghost, made by Firefly Aerospace, landed upright in Mare Crisium carrying 10 NASA experiments. It worked through a whole lunar day.
items.science: It drilled into the soil to measure heat flowing out of the Moon and filmed a sunset from the Moon's surface.
items.fact: It even watched a solar eclipse from the Moon, when Earth passed in front of the Sun.

items.name: Viking 1 lander
items.kid: Viking 1 was the first US spacecraft to land on Mars and send pictures from the ground. It worked for more than six years.
items.science: It tested Martian soil for signs of life and recorded weather every day, the first weather station on another planet.
items.fact: It landed exactly seven years after Apollo 11, on 20 July 1976.

items.name: Viking 2 lander
items.kid: Viking 2 landed on a rocky plain far to the north. In winter it took pictures of frost on the ground around it.
items.science: Its frost photos showed that water vapour in Mars's air freezes onto the surface each winter.
items.fact: Its landing spot, Utopia Planitia, is so far north the frost lasted for months.

items.name: Mars Pathfinder & Sojourner
items.kid: Pathfinder bounced onto Mars inside giant airbags, then let out Sojourner, a rover the size of a microwave oven: the first wheels on Mars.
items.science: Sojourner studied rocks that showed Mars once had floods of liquid water.
items.fact: Millions of people followed the mission online in 1997, a huge record for the early internet.

items.name: Mars Polar Lander (lost)
items.kid: Mars Polar Lander tried to land near the south pole, but contact was lost and it was never heard from again.
items.science: Studying what went wrong made later landers like Phoenix much safer.
items.fact: Engineers think its engines shut off too early, about 40 metres above the ground.

items.name: Spirit rover
items.kid: Spirit was planned to work for 90 days but kept going for six years, climbing hills in Gusev Crater. It finally got stuck in soft sand.
items.science: Its stuck wheel dug up almost pure silica, a sign of ancient hot springs, places where life could have lived.
items.fact: Engineers drove it backwards for years because one wheel stopped turning.

items.name: Opportunity rover
items.kid: Opportunity was also meant to last 90 days. It drove for over 14 years and 45 km, a marathon on another planet, until a huge dust storm covered its solar panels.
items.science: It found tiny round rocks called 'blueberries' and other proof that liquid water once soaked the ground.
items.fact: Its last message was turned into the words 'My battery is low and it's getting dark'.

items.name: Phoenix lander
items.kid: Phoenix landed in the Martian arctic and dug into the ground with a robotic arm. It found white chunks that slowly disappeared.
items.science: Those chunks were water ice turning straight into vapour: the first time we touched ice on Mars.
items.fact: It saw snow falling from Martian clouds.

items.name: Curiosity rover
items.kid: Curiosity is as big as a car and was lowered to the ground on ropes by a flying rocket 'sky crane'. It is still climbing a mountain called Mount Sharp.
items.science: It proved Gale Crater once held a lake with water that tiny life could have lived in.
items.fact: It sang 'Happy Birthday' to itself on Mars by vibrating its sample drill.

items.name: InSight lander
items.kid: InSight listened to the inside of Mars with a super-sensitive seismometer, like a doctor's stethoscope for a planet.
items.science: It recorded over 1,300 marsquakes and measured the size of Mars's core, crust and mantle for the first time.
items.fact: It even felt the shaking from meteorites hitting Mars.

items.name: Perseverance rover
items.kid: Perseverance is exploring Jezero Crater, an old lake with a river delta. It collects rock samples in tubes that a future mission could bring to Earth.
items.science: It is searching rocks from the ancient lake for signs of past microscopic life, and it made oxygen from Martian air.
items.fact: It carries the names of almost 11 million people on three small chips.

items.name: Ingenuity helicopter
items.kid: Ingenuity was a tiny helicopter that rode under Perseverance. It was supposed to fly 5 times and ended up flying 72 times!
items.science: It proved that aircraft can fly in Mars's very thin air, so future missions can scout from above.
items.fact: It carries a small piece of fabric from the Wright brothers' first aeroplane.

deep.name: Pioneer 10
deep.kid: The first spacecraft to fly past Jupiter. It is heading toward the star Aldebaran and will get there in about two million years.
deep.fact: It carries a gold plaque with a drawing of a man and a woman and a map showing where Earth is.

deep.name: Pioneer 11
deep.kid: The first spacecraft to visit Saturn. It also carries the famous gold plaque.
deep.fact: It flew through Saturn's rings area and showed it was safe for the Voyagers.

deep.name: Voyager 1
deep.kid: The farthest thing humans have ever made. In 2012 it left the Sun's bubble and entered interstellar space, and it still sends messages home.
deep.fact: It carries a Golden Record with music, greetings in 55 languages and sounds of Earth.

deep.name: Voyager 2
deep.kid: The only spacecraft to visit all four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. It entered interstellar space in 2018.
deep.fact: It launched 16 days BEFORE Voyager 1, but Voyager 1 took a faster path.

deep.name: New Horizons
deep.kid: It flew past Pluto in 2015 and showed us a heart-shaped glacier of frozen nitrogen. Then it visited Arrokoth, a snowman-shaped space rock.
deep.fact: It carries some of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, the man who discovered Pluto.
